title: Metrics and monitoring pipeline
summary: Design the system that collects millions of data points a minute, keeps recent ones fast to read and still alerts when parts of it fail. Compare Facebook's Gorilla, Google's Monarch and Uber's M3.

topics.role: Splits the series across machines so no single node holds them all, and lets a query fan out.
Keeps a second copy so a lost node or region does not lose recent data.
Frames the choice between a complete answer and an answer now when parts are unreachable.
Moves reads and shards to healthy machines when one fails.
Decides how points are encoded in memory and on disk.
Keeps the recent window in fast memory in front of slower history.

brief.text: A company runs thousands of services, and each one reports numbers about itself every few seconds. Engineers read them on dashboards, and automated checks watch them to raise alerts. Design the store behind this. It has to take a huge, steady stream of writes, answer recent queries almost instantly, and keep working when machines or a whole region fail, because it is what tells you that other things are failing.

requirements.label: 1. Write volume
requirements.value: 700 million data points added per minute

requirements.label: 2. Series count
requirements.value: 2 billion unique time series, each named by a string key

requirements.label: 4. Query load
requirements.value: More than 40,000 queries per second at peak

requirements.label: 5. Read speed
requirements.value: Reads succeed in under one millisecond

requirements.label: 6. Survive failure
requirements.value: Two in-memory replicas that are not co-located, and reads keep working when one server crashes

requirements.label: 7. No circular dependency
requirements.value: The monitoring system cannot depend on the storage systems it monitors for its alerting path

decisions.question: Where should the recent data live?

options.label: On disk behind a read-through cache
options.why: Cheap, but a dashboard asking for the newest point can miss the cache and fall through to the slow store.

options.label: In memory, as a write-through window of recent data, with history kept elsewhere
options.why: New points land in fast memory as they arrive, so the common recent query never touches the slow store.

options.label: In memory for everything, forever
options.why: Fast for all queries, but the cost of holding years of data in RAM is far beyond what the queries need.

realChoice.text: Gorilla acts as a write-through cache of the most recent 26 hours. The team saw that at least 85% of queries to its older store asked for data from the past 26 hours, so a window that size serves most reads.

decisions.question: A zone is cut off and some data cannot be reached. What should a query do?

options.label: Wait until every part answers, so the result is complete
options.why: Complete, but an outage then takes longer to notice, which defeats the point of monitoring.

options.label: Fail the query and ask the user to retry
options.why: Honest, but the dashboard or alert goes blank exactly when it is needed.

options.label: Return what it has and mark the result as possibly incomplete
options.why: The reader gets the freshest answer now and knows how far to trust it.

realChoice.text: Monarch trades consistency for availability and partition tolerance. It drops delayed writes, returns partial data for queries when needed, and flags that the data may be incomplete.

decisions.question: How should the copies be arranged?

options.label: Three replicas in one region written by quorum, with queries fanning out to other regions
options.why: Strong inside the region and cheap across regions, but a whole region loss takes its data with it until you query elsewhere.

options.label: One copy in memory, rebuilt from disk after a failure
options.why: Simplest and cheapest, but a crash leaves a gap where reads cannot be served.

options.label: Two independent full copies in different regions, each fed in parallel
options.why: Either region can answer alone, and a region failure is handled by reading from the other.

realChoice.text: Gorilla keeps two completely independent instances in separate regions. A write is streamed to each with no attempt to guarantee consistency, and reads go to the closest available one. When one region fails, reads are retried in the other.

decisions.question: How does data get from the thing being measured into the store?

options.label: The store discovers each source and pulls from it
options.why: The store controls the pace, but it needs discovery services and proxies for every source.

options.label: A central poller scrapes every source on a schedule
options.why: Easy to reason about, but one poller becomes the bottleneck and the single point of failure.

options.label: Each source pushes its data to the store
options.why: Sources only need an address to send to, which removes the discovery machinery.

realChoice.text: Early versions of Monarch discovered monitored entities and pulled from them, which needed discovery services and proxies and hurt scalability. Moving to push removed those dependencies.

decisions.question: Where should the data be reduced to a coarser form?

options.label: In a nightly batch job over stored data
options.why: Easy to run, but every point is stored raw first and the job must read it all back.

options.label: At query time, over the raw points
options.why: Nothing is lost, but each dashboard repeats the same expensive reduction.

options.label: At collection time, as the points arrive
options.why: The reduction happens once, and nothing has to be pulled back out of storage to do it.

realChoice.text: M3 downsamples at the time of collection. Doing it later would mean pulling large volumes of stored data back out, which costs network, CPU and disk. Storage policies pick retention and downsampling by matching a metric's tags.

diagram.title: Metrics pipeline: writers, ingest, in-memory store, a second copy and the query path

nodes.label: Writers and agents
nodes.tradeoff: Gorilla's write clients buffer one minute of data while shards move and drop older points to make room for newer ones. It prefers recent data over complete data.

nodes.label: Ingest (push)
nodes.tradeoff: Sources push to Monarch, which removes the discovery services and proxies that pulling needed. Separately, Monarch drops delayed writes rather than wait on them.

nodes.label: Aggregation at collection
nodes.tradeoff: M3 downsamples as data is collected, so nothing is read back later. The cost is that a rule can only roll up metrics from one Prometheus instance for now, as of the 2018 post.

nodes.label: Shard map
nodes.tradeoff: A Paxos-based ShardManager assigns shards to nodes and spreads a failed node's shards over the rest. Writers wait in a buffer during the move.

nodes.label: In-memory store
nodes.tradeoff: Recent data is held in RAM, compressed to an average of 1.37 bytes per point instead of 16. Anything older has to come from another store.

nodes.label: Second copy, other region
nodes.tradeoff: Each region gets every write with no attempt at consistency, so either can answer alone. The two copies can disagree.

nodes.label: Long-term store
nodes.tradeoff: M3 lets a metric's tags choose its retention and resolution, such as 2 days raw or 30 days at one minute. Coarser data lasts longer but loses detail.

nodes.label: Query tier
nodes.tradeoff: Monarch queries run through a root, zone and leaf tree and can return partial results. A result may be fast and incomplete.

nodes.label: Alerting
nodes.tradeoff: Monarch keeps data in memory so alerts do not depend on storage systems that themselves rely on monitoring. The price is the cost of RAM.

compare:
Gorilla and Monarch both keep the newest data in memory, and both accept an incomplete answer sooner than a blocked one. Gorilla writes to two regions without trying to make them agree, and Monarch drops late writes and returns partial query results. M3 adds a third design for retention: it downsamples as data arrives.

They split on copies and reach. Gorilla keeps two independent full instances in separate regions. M3 writes each metric to three replicas inside one region by quorum and sends queries out to remote regions rather than replicating across them. Monarch splits its data into 38 zones and joins them with a global query tree, and its recovery log is written on a best-effort basis so the system keeps running if the file systems behind it are down.

Read the dates with care. Gorilla is a 2015 paper and holds a 26-hour window in front of a separate long-term store. Monarch is a 2020 paper describing Google's system. M3 is a 2018 post. Each describes its system at that time.

quiz.question: Why did Gorilla's team reject a separate Memcache write-through cache for recent data?
options: It could not hold data for 26 hours
Appending to a series needs a read and a write, which would flood the cache server with traffic
It did not support replication across regions
quiz.why: Adding a point to an existing series would require a read/write cycle, and that causes extremely high traffic to the cache server.
wrong: The reason given is traffic, not capacity.
The paper's objection is the append cycle, not regions.

quiz.question: Monarch cannot reach part of its data during a network partition. What does it do with a query?
options: Blocks until every zone has answered, so the result is complete
Rejects the query so that nobody acts on a partial picture
Returns partial data and flags it as possibly incomplete
quiz.why: Monarch drops delayed writes and returns partial data, with a mechanism to show that the data may be incomplete.
wrong: Blocking would delay detection of the very outage being investigated.
Rejecting leaves dashboards and alerts blank when they are most needed.

quiz.question: A Gorilla node dies and its shards are being reassigned. What happens to the points still arriving?
options: Writers buffer about a minute and drop older points
They queue on disk for as long as the node stays down, then replay
They go only to the instance in the other region and nowhere else
quiz.why: The buffers hold one minute of data and discard older points to make room for newer ones, which usually covers the shard move.
wrong: Gorilla favours recent data over a full backlog.
Writes are streamed to both instances; the buffer covers the move in the same region.

quiz.question: What lets Gorilla fit a point in an average of 1.37 bytes instead of 16?
options: Sampling less often than the 15-second granularity it requires
Keeping only the newest value of each series, since older ones live elsewhere
Delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR of values
quiz.why: These two encodings compress each series as a stream, down to 1.37 bytes per point on average, a 12x reduction.
wrong: The 15-second granularity is a stated requirement, not a saving.
Gorilla keeps a window of points for each series.

quiz.question: Why does M3 downsample at the time of collection?
options: Raw points cannot be stored in M3DB at all, so they must be reduced first
Later rollups mean pulling large volumes of stored data back out
It removes the need for any per-metric retention rules at all
quiz.why: Downsampling later needs the same read-then-aggregate work as a compaction, so M3 avoids it by reducing data as it arrives and saves network, CPU and disk IO.
wrong: M3 has a policy of 2 days with no downsampling, so raw data is kept.
Rules still pick retention and resolution by matching tags.

quiz.question: How does Uber's M3 give one view across regions without replicating across them?
options: Metrics stay in the local region, and queries fan out to remote ones
Every region writes synchronously to every other region, so each holds a full copy
A central region copies all of the data each night for global queries
quiz.why: Replication stays inside a region, and a query fans out to local and remote M3DB instances and coordinators and returns compressed blocks.
wrong: Cross-region replication is the cost M3 avoids.
M3 does not describe a nightly copy.
